title: Two bar charts, two questions: how much CO2 per unit heat, and does the flame stay inside the material limit?
summary: The CO2-intensity chart is a bookkeeping result: carbon in per kilojoule out. The peak-temperature chart is a constraint check against a dashed limit line. Read them together: the first says how far substitution helps, the second says whether the hardware survives it.

media.alt: Bar chart of tuyere CO2 intensity in g CO2 per kJ: base case coal only 0.121 in grey, 80 percent CH4 substitution 0.091 in orange, 80 percent H2 substitution 0.067 in blue, with an arrow noting 45 percent lower at 80 percent H2.

source.caption: CO2 intensity vs. substitution level
group: 09_peak_temperature: Peak temperature vs. the 2400K tuyere material limit
source.note: Group explainer for the two result charts. The CO2 chart is built from stated stoichiometry; the temperature chart reports peak flame temperatures from the 2D reacting-flow cases against a 2400 K allowable limit. See 'As drawn' for a consistency check that the owner should review.

read_the_figure.question: How much does CO2 per unit of heat fall as coal is replaced by CH4 or H2, and is the peak flame temperature within what the tuyere material allows?
read_the_figure.axes: Figure 08: categories on x (base case with coal only, 80% CH4 substitution, 80% H2 substitution); y is CO2 intensity in grams of CO2 per kilojoule of heat released, linear from 0 to 0.14. Figure 09: categories on x (base case with 15 mm lance, base case with 25 mm lance, 10% CH4, 10% H2, 80% H2); y is peak flame temperature in kelvin from 0 to 5000, with a dashed red horizontal line at 2400 K.
look_at: Bar heights are labelled with their values: 0.121, 0.091, 0.067 g/kJ and 3100, 2700, 3040, 4500, 3550 K. Because the y axes start at zero the heights compare honestly.
The blue arrow on figure 08 says '45% lower at 80% H2'. Check it: 0.067 / 0.121 = 0.554, so the reduction is 44.6 percent, which rounds to 45.
The dashed line in figure 09 is the limit. Count how many bars stand above it: all five do.
Colour carries the fuel: grey base case, orange methane, blue hydrogen. The two cases use different categories in the two charts (80% CH4 appears only in 08, 10% CH4 and 10% H2 only in 09).
read_the_figure.proves: That, under the study's own accounting, substituting fuel lowers CO2 per kJ, and that in the reported 2D cases every peak temperature is above the 2400 K limit. It does not prove either number is right: neither chart shows uncertainty or the model behind it.
if_wrong: A reduction larger than the heat share replaced would mean the accounting counts something other than heat.

A peak temperature far above the adiabatic flame temperature of the mixture points to a modelling artefact (for example very high local equivalence ratio, a missing radiation or heat-loss term, or a single hot cell) rather than a physical flame.
Bars that differ in two things at once (fuel and substitution level) cannot isolate the effect of either.
must_check: The basis of 'per kJ': heat released, lower or higher heating value, and whether the substitution percentage is by heat, by mass or by the rating of the injection system.
The same cases in both charts, so that CO2 and temperature can be matched case by case.
Peak temperature is a maximum over cells, which is a noisy statistic; a mean or a profile along the axis is more robust.
Whether the 2400 K limit refers to the gas or the wall: the wall is cooler than the flame, so comparing a gas peak with a wall limit is conservative.
That all conditions except the one varied are held fixed between bars.
as_drawn: CO2 intensity of pure carbon burning to CO2 is 44.01 / 393.5 = 0.112 g/kJ, using the standard enthalpy of 393.5 kJ/mol. The base-case bar (0.121) is about 8 percent higher than this bound, which a coal with volatiles and ash should not exceed on a total-heat basis. The basis of the number needs checking.

If a fraction s of the heat comes from a fuel with intensity i and the rest from coal at 0.121, the blend is (1 - s) 0.121 + s i. For H2 (i = 0) the bar 0.067 implies s = 0.45; for CH4 (i = 44.01 / 802.3 = 0.055 g/kJ, lower heating value) the bar 0.091 implies s = 0.45 too. Both bars are consistent with a heat share of about 45 percent, not 80 percent. If 80 percent of the heat came from the substitute the blends would be 0.024 (H2) and 0.068 (CH4) g/kJ.
The most likely explanation is that '80 percent' is a share of something other than the total heat release, for example of the rating of the injection system; the figure does not say.

Peak temperatures: 3100 K and 2700 K for the 15 mm and 25 mm base cases, 3040 K at 10% CH4, 4500 K at 10% H2 and 3550 K at 80% H2. A stoichiometric hydrogen-air flame from room-temperature reactants reaches about 2400 K as a textbook value; preheating and oxygen enrichment raise that by hundreds of kelvin, not to 4500 K. Values this high are a flag for a modelling artefact and should be treated as such.

terms.meaning: Mass of CO2 emitted per unit of heat released by combustion.
The share of the original fuel input that is replaced by another fuel. The basis (heat, mass, rating) must be stated.
Heat released by complete combustion with the water leaving as vapour.
The fixed ratios of reactants and products in a balanced reaction. It fixes how many grams of CO2 come from a gram of fuel.
The highest gas temperature in the computed field. It is the maximum over many cells, so one outlier sets it.
The temperature reached by burning a mixture with no heat loss. It is an upper bound for a steady flame in that mixture.
The temperature the nozzle material can stand in service; here 2400 K.

remember: Hydrogen produces no CO2 at the point of use, so CO2 intensity falls linearly with the share of heat supplied by it.
Methane makes about half the CO2 per kJ of pure carbon: 44.01/802.3 is 0.055 g/kJ against 0.112.
Percent substitution needs a basis: heat, mass or rating.
A flame cannot be hotter than its adiabatic flame temperature; a result above it needs explaining.
A bar chart with a limit line is a constraint check: look at the bars, not the heights alone.

understand.title: Why intensity is a weighted average
understand.text: CO2 per kJ is total CO2 over total heat. If a share s of the heat comes from fuel B, the total is the heat-weighted average of the two fuels' intensities. That is a straight line from the coal value (s = 0) to the pure-fuel value (s = 1). A figure that departs from the line has changed the definition.

understand.title: Why hydrogen is more dangerous for the nozzle
understand.text: Hydrogen burns fast and close to the lance, so the heat release sits where the material is. The chart shows the temperature side of that trade: the CO2 gain is bought with a hotter, more concentrated flame in the reported cases.

steps.title: CO2 per kJ of a pure fuel
steps.note: One mole of carbon gives one mole of CO2 (44.01 g). Standard molar heats: 393.5 kJ for carbon, 802.3 kJ for methane (lower heating value). Hydrogen has no carbon. Checked numerically.

steps.title: Blend by heat share
steps.note: Heat-weighted average. s is the fraction of the total heat supplied by the substitute.

steps.title: Relative reduction
steps.note: This is the 45 percent printed on the arrow. It is a check you can do from the labels alone.

steps.title: Inverting for the implied share
steps.note: Given a bar value, what share of heat does it imply? For H2 this gives 0.45, for CH4 also 0.45: compare with the stated 80 percent.

steps.title: Temperature rise from a heat release
steps.note: A rough energy balance with fuel mass fraction Y_F and a mean specific heat c_p. It ignores dissociation, which lowers the real value at high temperature; that is why 4500 K is hard to reach in a real flame.

steps.title: Which bars break the limit
steps.note: A negative margin means the peak exceeds the limit. In figure 09 all five bars have negative margins, from -300 K (25 mm base) to -2100 K (10% H2). Computed from the labels.

worked.title: What heat share does a bar imply?
worked.problem: CH4 at 0.055 g/kJ replaces coal at 0.121 g/kJ and the blend is 0.091 g/kJ. What share of the heat comes from methane?
worked.answer: About 45 percent of the heat, not the stated 80 percent. Either the substitution percentage is defined on another basis or the chart's basis differs; the owner should confirm.

analyze.q: Both bars imply the same heat share, about 45 percent. What does that coincidence suggest about how the cases were set up?
analyze.hint: One definition applied to both fuels.

analyze.q: 10% H2 gives 4500 K but 80% H2 gives 3550 K. Give a physical reason that more hydrogen could mean a lower peak, and a numerical reason.
analyze.hint: Dilution and heat-release location versus a single hot cell.

analyze.q: The 25 mm lance gives 2700 K and the 15 mm gives 3100 K. Is the 25 mm case acceptable?
analyze.hint: Compare each with the 2400 K line.

evaluate.q: Is it fair to say 'substitution lowers CO2 by 45 percent' from this chart? State the extra information you would ask for.
evaluate.hint: Basis of the percentage and of 'per kJ'.

evaluate.q: The conclusion drawn from the chart is that materials, not chemistry, set the ceiling. How much does that rest on peak temperatures that may be artefacts?
evaluate.hint: Think of the adiabatic bound and the maximum-over-cells statistic.

create: Redraw figure 08 as a line from 0 to 100 percent heat share for both fuels with the blend equation, and mark the reported bars.
Redraw figure 09 with the adiabatic flame temperature of each mixture as a second marker, and a bar of the wall temperature, so that the limit is compared with the right quantity.

checks.q: Why does CO2 intensity from hydrogen come out as zero at the point of use?
checks.hint: Look at the formula of hydrogen.
checks.answer: Hydrogen contains no carbon, so burning it produces water only; any CO2 comes from the remaining coal.

checks.q: Check the arrow on figure 08: how much lower is 0.067 than 0.121?
If 80 percent of the heat came from hydrogen and coal gave 0.121 g/kJ, what intensity would you expect?
checks.answer: (1 - 0.8) x 0.121 = 0.024 g/kJ, much lower than 0.067, so the charted cases cannot be 80 percent by heat.

checks.q: Why should a peak of 4500 K make you suspicious?
checks.hint: Compare with the adiabatic flame temperature of hydrogen in air.
checks.answer: A flame cannot exceed its adiabatic flame temperature, about 2400 K from room-temperature stoichiometric hydrogen-air (textbook value); preheat and enrichment raise it by hundreds of kelvin, not to 4500, so the value probably reflects a modelling artefact.

checks.q: What extra bar would make figure 09 a fair test against the limit?
checks.hint: What temperature does the material see?
checks.answer: The wall or material temperature next to the lance, computed with heat transfer, alongside the gas peak; or a mean gas temperature near the nozzle instead of a single-cell maximum.

provenance.opened_image: 2026-10-06, figures 08 and 09 opened at full resolution (about 1400 and 1600 px wide)
provenance.notes: Standard theory only. The bar values are printed on the figures. Two consistency findings are for the owner: (1) the bars imply a heat share of about 45 percent for both fuels, not the stated 80 percent; (2) the base-case 0.121 g/kJ exceeds the 0.112 g/kJ pure-carbon bound, and the 4500 K peak is above any plausible adiabatic flame temperature. The explainer reports these neutrally; the owner should decide whether to correct the figure or its caption.
